newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Lebanon courts foreign investors at Swiss forum.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon courts foreign investors at Swiss forum.

text.p: Lebanon, seeking to return to its glory days as a financial, commercial and tourism centre, appealed to Western businessmen at a Swiss forum to take advantage of investment incentives it is offering.

Economy Minister Yassin Jaber told the Crans Montana forum that Lebanon, which has embarked on a huge drive to rebuild the country from the ruins of the 1975-1990 civil war, offered a unique location as a gateway to the Middle east, liberal regulations, skilled workforce and modern infrastructure.

"Lebanon wants to regain its shining past and has ambitions to play a more active role than the one it played before," he told the forum in the Swiss mountain resort of Crans Montana. "Lessons have been learnt -- some economic and some political."
Jaber said Lebanon offered great investment potential with its liberal regulatory system where he said tax rates were among the lowest in the world.
He said Lebanon had 83 registered commercial and specialised banks and 90 insurance companies operating in an environment where corporate and income tax rates had a 10 percent ceiling.

Free zones in the country were also exempt from customs duties for imports of goods and equipment. The government was also considering a 10-year tax break for foreign businesses operating in these zones.

Lebanon's national reconstruction campaign has won the blessing of World Bank President James Wolfensohn, who announced a big increase in funding during a visit this month and declared his backing for Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri's much criticised deficit financing of national reconstruction.

Wolfensohn announced the bank and its private sector arm, the International Finance Corporation (IFC), allocated a total $420 million to Lebanon in 1997. The bank also increased emergency funding by $50 million to a total of $150 million.

The reconstruction drive has sent Lebanon's total debt soaring to 17.5 trillion Lebanese pounds ($11.4 billion) from five trillion at the end of 1993. This is nearly 83 percent of estimated GDP of $13.9 billion at end 1996, official data show.
